# mcp-cassette

> The cassette is itself an MCP server, so any client in any language connects to it exactly as it connects to the live one: no library to import, no product code to change, no transport to wrap.

Record one session against a real Model Context Protocol server, then run agent
tests against the recording with no credentials, no rate limits and no network.
The same binary gates a tool contract against breaking changes and lints for
poisoning every model-facing text a server publishes. That lint is the prompt
injection check: a tool description, a prompt template and a resource listing
are untrusted input an agent reads as instructions, so `check` looks for the
instruction overrides, concealment directives and exfiltration URLs a
tool-poisoning attack needs to work.

## Install

```
npm install -g mcp-cassette
```

Or run without installing: `npx mcp-cassette <command>`. Node.js >= 20.

## Commands

- `record -o <file> -- <server command>`: sit between a client and a live server, write every message to a cassette. `--redact-config <file>` adds your own redaction rules.
- `replay <cassette>`: serve the cassette as a real MCP server on stdio, or over Streamable HTTP with `--listen <host:port>`. `--volatile <json-pointer>` declares a request field that changes every run, repeatable.
- `check --stdio "<server command>"`: validate handshake and schemas, lint for poisoning the tool descriptions and schemas, the prompt and prompt-argument descriptions, and the names and descriptions of resources and resource templates. Findings on every surface but tools are reported at `warn` whatever their rule's level, and graduate to it no earlier than the next minor. `--format text|json|sarif`. Two gates: `--fail-on error|warn` covers every finding, and `--lint-fail-on error|warn|never` covers the `CAS-L` description lint alone, defaulting to whatever `--fail-on` is. Exit 1 on a finding at or above its gate; `--lint-fail-on never` reports every lint finding and gates on none, while a structural `CAS-C` finding still fails. Exit 2 at every level when the server could not be inspected at all.
- `snapshot --stdio "<server command>"`: write the tool contract to a file. With `--check`, diff a live server against it and exit 1 on a breaking change.
- `verify <cassette> -- <server command>`: re-fire recorded requests at a live server and diff the answers.
- `redact <cassette>`: redact secrets in an existing cassette, or `--scan` to audit without writing. `--redact-config <file>` adds your own rules, and `--check-config` analyses their patterns for catastrophic backtracking.
- `lint <cassette> [--json]`: check a cassette header against its own frames, check the header's newer fields (`volatile` must be a list of valid declarations, `redaction.configHash` must be a sha256 hex digest), and scan what the recorded server returned for indirect prompt injection. Output scanning reads the answers to `tools/call`, `tasks/get`, `tasks/result`, `resources/read` and `prompts/get` with six rules (CAS-L001, L003, L006, L009, L010, L013); the two task methods are read because a task-augmented call delivers its result there. The `intent` rules are excluded by their own premise, a result that mentions a shell being a result about a shell, and six `shape` rules are excluded because they fire on ordinary returned data. CAS-L006 is narrowed on this surface to a run of two or more invisible code points or any Tags-block code point, because a lone zero-width character is what a web editor leaves in real issue bodies; the declaration-side rule is unchanged. A base64 `blob` or image `data` is never decoded or scanned, and text inside a redaction placeholder is not scanned. Findings name the request id, the method and the JSON path. Exit 1 on a header that contradicts its frames and on nothing else: the output and header-field findings are `warn`, reported and never gated. No `--format sarif`: a cassette has no server, tool count or gate to put in one.

Every finding carries a stable rule id in parentheses. Match on the id, not the wording.

- [Site](https://mcpcassette.dev/): the same material as a page.
- [How replay works](https://mcpcassette.dev/replay/): why a cassette serves any client in any language, the WHATWG event-stream parsing rules, the two protocol lifecycles a cassette tells apart, and the deferred header.
- [Cassette format v2](https://github.com/ivermin1123/mcp-cassette/blob/main/docs/cassette-format-v2.md): the on-disk format.
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/ivermin1123/mcp-cassette/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md): what changed and what breaks.

## What it does not do

- A replay answers from the recording, so it cannot compare models or servers and cannot tell you whether a live server still behaves that way. Use `verify` for that.
- `snapshot --check` does not resolve `$ref`, and does not cover `anyOf`/`oneOf`/`allOf`, constraint direction (`minimum`, `pattern`, `format`), or `outputSchema`. It reports an unresolved reference plainly instead of guessing.
- The safety lint reads text, so `intent` rules cannot separate a hostile description from a legitimate one that really does describe running commands. Those stay `warn`.
- `check --url` and `snapshot --url` against Streamable HTTP are marked experimental; stdio is the supported path.
- Replay is a test double, not a conformance checker. A missing session id, or an `Mcp-Method`, `MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Name` or `Mcp-Param-*` the body contradicts, is a warning on stderr, never a protocol error. Replay holds no `inputSchema`, so it judges a mismatched custom header and not a missing one.
- Replay reproduces notifications the server initiated, at their recorded position: a frame is anchored to the last client request whose answer preceded it, or, when it was recorded while a request was still outstanding, to that request, where it is emitted just before the answer. A frame whose anchor the client never sends is reported rather than emitted. Server-to-client requests (legacy sampling, elicitation, roots) are recorded but not originated, and replay prints how many to stderr. Under 2026-07-28, those flows arrive as `input_required` results instead (MRTR), so they are replayed.
- Replay matching is exact by default: a request whose fingerprint was never recorded is a miss. `--on-miss warn` may answer it with another recording of the same method, naming the diverging paths on stderr each time, so under warn a call with different arguments can receive another call's answer. Two requests never borrow: an MRTR retry, which matches exactly, including `inputResponses` and `requestState`, or misses; and a `tasks/get`, because the next unused poll is an answer about a different task.
- Redaction rules are configurable: `--redact-config <file>` holds `{ patterns: [{ name, regex }], keys: [...], allow: [...] }`, where `patterns` adds token shapes (the name becomes the placeholder label, lowercase letters, never a built-in name, compiled global, `i` and `u` flags only), `keys` adds names whose values are secrets whatever their shape, and `allow` exempts specific values the built-in rules over-redact. The same file must go to `record` and to `replay`: redaction runs before fingerprinting, so a cassette carries a hash of the config it was recorded under and replay refuses one whose hash does not match, naming which side is missing a config, and `redact` refuses to rewrite such a cassette under any other config. The hash holds neither the regexes nor the allowed values, but it is not a secret: an unsalted sha256 of a small document can be confirmed offline by anyone with a candidate config, so `allow` is for already-public values. It is taken over what the config does, not how it was written, so reordering or recasing `keys` does not invalidate a cassette. A pattern that matches the empty string is refused, and no pattern may rewrite text inside a placeholder, so redaction stays idempotent. An older mcp-cassette ignores the field and replays with the built-in rules. Custom patterns run over attacker-controlled server output, so `redact --check-config` analyses them with the optional `recheck` peer and exits non-zero when one is not proven linear-time.
- A request field that changes every run (a timestamp, a generated id) can be declared instead of tolerated: `replay --volatile /arguments/requestedAt`, repeatable, optionally scoped to one method as `tools/call:/arguments/requestedAt`, and the same list may live in the cassette header as `volatile`, which the flags add to. Declared pointers are dropped from both sides before matching and before the miss diagnosis, so a request differing only in one of them matches and a miss never blames one. This is the precise version of what `--on-miss warn` gives approximately; everything else still matches exactly.
- `subscriptions/listen` (2026-07-28) is answered by its recorded acknowledgment, held open, and fed its recorded change notifications at their recorded positions; the subscription id is re-keyed to the client's own listen request id.
- Over a 2026-07-28 HTTP server, `check`, `snapshot` and `verify --url` mirror the body into the headers the transport requires: `Mcp-Method` always, `Mcp-Name` on `tools/call`, `resources/read` and `prompts/get`, and `Mcp-Param-{name}` for every tool parameter whose schema carries `x-mcp-header`. Those are resolved from `tools/list` before any `tools/call`, so `verify` lists once when the cassette calls a tool and calls without the headers when the server cannot list. A value travels plain when it is plain ASCII with no leading or trailing whitespace, and as `=?base64?...?=` otherwise. A tool whose `x-mcp-header` declarations break the spec's constraints is withheld by the calling path only: `verify` leaves it out of its header resolution, names it on stderr and re-fires the call without `Mcp-Param-*`, while `check` keeps the tool, lints it as before and reports the declaration as `CAS-C008` at `warn`, and `snapshot` keeps it in the contract. `CAS-C008` is reported on every target, stdio included, because the declaration belongs to the schema and not to the wire. On stdio and in the legacy era nothing is mirrored and nothing is withheld.
